accuracy.evidence: Pitch is modelled from real physics: a clamped ruler's frequency scales with 1/L squared, a band's rises with tension and falls with thickness, and a blown bottle's air column gives f proportional to 1/(air length), so more water gives a higher note. The drum keeps the same frequency when hit harder and only the amplitude and loudness bar change. Statements match the Year 4 Sound programme of study wording on pitch and volume.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented sound slips: high means loud and low means quiet, thick or big objects make higher notes, the most air gives the highest note, bigger vibrations mean higher pitch, and sound without vibration. The adult text also flags the blowing versus tapping bottle reversal. Every wrong Challenge answer has its own message naming the slip with a reason about vibration speed or size.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagpitch is built on vibration speed: a ruler over a table edge animates at a rate set by its length, an elastic band is tuned by thickness and tension, four bottles are blown and ordered by note, and a drum shows a loudness bar moving while the pitch dot stays still. It differs from flagloud, which is about loud and quiet for ages 3 to 4, and from flagwave; shingle overlap is under the 30% gate.

lab_teaches.evidence: The six steps build in order: length and pitch with the ruler, thickness and tightness with a band, air column length with bottles, loudness versus pitch with a drum, applying the patterns to sort six objects, then a mixed Challenge. A pitch meter shows each note's position so the pattern is visible even with sound off, and Show me completes every step in under 2 s.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions come before the action they test: what happens to the twang when the ruler sticks out less, which band makes the highest note, which bottle is highest when blown (the most-air trap), and what changes when a drum is hit harder (the loud-means-high trap). The result on screen confirms or corrects each guess straight away.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The Challenge asks six questions: a shorter ruler's pitch, the lowest elastic band, what a harder drum hit changes, the highest blown bottle, what makes every sound, and what faster vibrations do. Each distractor maps to a named slip message (lower, thintight, highloud, moreair, hot, fastquiet) that explains in one or two plain sentences why it is wrong.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs score FK grade 2.1 with short sentences and things a child can try: a ruler, elastic bands, a whistle and a drum. The adult text is FK 5.4 and uses the curriculum words vibration, pitch, volume and frequency. Lab prompts are one short line each, and pitch meter labels say high, middle and low in plain words.

no_filler.evidence: No filler words pass the content gate; every paragraph carries a fact, a method or a named mistake. The family tip is a concrete home test with a box, elastic bands and a ruler plus two exact questions to ask, the key idea states the speed-pitch and size-loudness rules once, and hints name the one feature to compare.

mobile.evidence: The browser walk passed on iPhone 13 and desktop with no console errors. Every canvas action has a large button twin (Shorter, Longer, Twang, Thinner, Thicker, Tighter, Looser, Pluck, Bottle 1 to 4, Soft hit, Hard hit, High pitch, Low pitch), so the lab works with taps alone. Phone screenshots in both themes show the ruler, bottles, drum and meter fitting the width.

accessibility.evidence: axe passes in light and dark themes. The canvas has a live aria-label that says what happened, such as 15 cm: fast vibrations, a high note, so the pattern is available without sound or sight. Notes only play when the sound button is on, the pitch meter shows results visually for deaf users, colours come from A.col and motion is skipped under reduced motion.
